ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act); Companies Act 1993 (ss. 20–24 name reservation; ss. 82–90 director and shareholder registers); Financial Markets Authority AML/CFT Code of Practice 2011; Counter-Terrorism Act 2002; Russia Sanctions Act 2022 and Russia Sanctions Regulations 2022; Companies (Disclose Beneficial Ownership Information) Amendment Bill (registered beneficial ownership regime in legislative process); administered by the Companies Office (MBIE), the Financial Markets Authority, the Department of Internal Affairs, and the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified copy of valid passport of each director and beneficial owner (UBO)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Issuing passport authority of country of origin (or notary public certifying the copy)

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of No Criminal Record (Police Clearance) for each director and UBO
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: National Police / Ministry of Justice of country of origin

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate registry of the corporate shareholder's country of origin

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Proof of residential or operational address (utility bill or bank statement) for each director and UBO, and for the proposed registered office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Licensed utility provider, bank, or licensed virtual office provider

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, shareholders, UBOs and proposed authorized signatories against: (1) the New Zealand Consolidated Sanctions List administered by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT); (2) the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List; (3) the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, required given the designated payment rails of USD wire transfers and Wise B2B; (4) the United Kingdom Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (ONSI) consolidated list; (5) the consolidated financial sanctions lists of the European Union; (6) the FATF High-Risk Jurisdictions Subject to a Call for Action list; and (7) domestic criminal-history and global adverse-media databases per the AML/CFT Act 2009 and FMA/DIA guidance. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) is triggered on any PEP identification; domestic and foreign PEPs must be monitored for 12 months following cessation of public office; suspicious transaction reports must be filed with the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit under s. 40 of the AML/CFT Act 2009.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Register (Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment) — online registration portal at www.companiesoffice.govt.nz
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be stated in English or te reo Māori using Latin (Roman) script. Permitted characters are letters A–Z, numerals 0–9, and the punctuation set & ' + , - . / ( ). Māori macron vowels (ā, ē, ī, ō, ū) are accepted in te reo Māori names. Foreign script characters (CJK, Cyrillic, Arabic, etc.) are not accepted; a transliterated or translated romanized trading name may be filed as an 'other name', but the registered legal name must be in Latin script. The legal name must end with 'Limited' or the approved abbreviation 'Ltd' (full stop optional); no other corporate suffix is permitted. Names must not be identical or virtually identical to an existing or reserved name on the Companies Register, must not be offensive, misleading, or imply Crown/government affiliation.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Limited (otherwise than as the statutory suffix)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection of a name under s. 20 of the Companies Act 1993, the applicant shall: (1) resubmit an alternative name via the Companies Register online portal at no cost; (2) file a written request for reconsideration with the Registrar of Companies, Companies Office, within 20 working days of the rejection, stating the grounds on which the name is acceptable; (3) if the Registrar confirms the refusal, appeal to the High Court of New Zealand under s. 24 of the Companies Act 1993 within 20 working days of the confirmation decision by filing an originating application under the High Court Rules 2016. A reserved name lapses after the 20-working-day reservation period if incorporation is not completed; the name may be re-reserved immediately by re-filing if still available.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for Companies Office compliance: s. 193 of the Companies Act 1993 requires a physical street address in New Zealand that is not a post office box; a licensed virtual office or registered agent with a physical address and mail-forwarding service satisfies this requirement. However, the target payment rails (Wise B2B and wire transfers) require contracting banks and payment processors to perform KYC, and a mailbox-only address may materially delay bank account opening. For this remote BPO call-centre model, the New Zealand registered office must not be represented as the operational headquarters, because central management and control in New Zealand would create New Zealand tax residence under the Income Tax Act 2007 and could undermine the Tax_Exempt_Zone operating position for foreign-source income.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low: approximately 5–10% per annum probability of a registry-based verification event. The New Zealand Companies Office conducts documentary verification rather than routine unannounced field inspections; Inland Revenue audits are triggered by tax-residency indicators; FMA/DIA AML/CFT on-site inspections apply only if the entity is a reporting entity under the AML/CFT Act 2009, which a non-resident BPO company without New Zealand financial activities is not.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No 105), ss 12-14 (incorporation, certificate and effect), ss 19-24 (company name), ss 25-34 (constitution), ss 38-46 (share issues and no-par-value shares), ss 83-92 (share register and statutory records), ss 87-90 (directors' register), ss 128-151 (board of directors, duties, consents and residential requirements), s 189 (registered office); Companies Act 1993 Regulations 1994; New Zealand Business Number Act 2016; Tax Administration Act 1994; Goods and Services Tax Act 1985. Note: New Zealand law provides one uniform statutory category of limited liability company; the designation 'International Company' (CK_IC) is a commercial and offshore operating label and does not create a separate statutory vehicle.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office - Registrar of Companies, a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), Wellington, administered online through the ONESTOP Business Registration Service and the Companies Online portal.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form 1 - Application for Registration of a Company, lodged electronically under s 12 of the Companies Act 1993 and the Companies Act 1993 Regulations 1994.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital and no escrow-account or capital-deposit requirement. New Zealand shares are issued of no par value (s 39) and the initial allotment may be fully paid, partly paid or unpaid, provided the share register and Form 1 allocation schedule accurately record the agreed consideration, which may be cash, property, services or a combination.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION OF [●] NEW ZEALAND LIMITED (ADOPTED IN WRITING BY THE SOLE DIRECTOR PURSUANT TO S 91 OF THE COMPANIES ACT 1993)
A. SHARE CAPITAL SUBSCRIPTION
1. RESOLVED THAT the authorised capital structure of the Company comprise 1,000 ordinary shares of no par value, and that 1,000 ordinary shares be allotted and issued as fully paid to [●] (the 'Subscriber'), being the sole subscriber named in Form 1, in consideration for [cash subscription of NZD 1,000 / transfer of equipment and initial working capital], which consideration the board values as adequate and fair.
2. RESOLVED THAT the share register (s 83) be updated accordingly and that any share certificates be executed by the Company in accordance with the constitution.
B. REGISTERED OFFICE ADOPTION
3. RESOLVED THAT the registered office of the Company be, and is hereby, fixed at [street address, suburb, city, New Zealand], being a physical address in New Zealand available for service of legal documents and documents issued by the Registrar of Companies (s 189), and that the directors are authorised to file the registered-office particulars through the Companies Office.
C. OFFICER APPOINTMENTS
4. RESOLVED THAT [Full Name], [passport / national ID number], of [residential address], be and is hereby appointed as the sole director of the Company, with all powers, duties and authorities conferred by the Companies Act 1993 and the constitution, to hold office until the first annual shareholders' meeting or earlier resignation or removal in accordance with s 152.
5. RESOLVED THAT the appointment of [Full Name] as Company Secretary is approved for administrative purposes only; the board acknowledges that a company secretary is not a statutory requirement in New Zealand.
6. RESOLVED THAT the director (and the company secretary, if appointed) be and are hereby jointly and severally authorised to open one or more bank accounts with a licensed New Zealand bank, to complete NZBN and Inland Revenue registrations, to execute BPO client agreements and telecommunications contracts for the call-centre business (ISIC 7820 / NAICS 561422), and to appoint legal counsel, tax advisers and incorporation agents as necessary to give effect to the formation of the Company.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Company Name Clearance and Availability Pre-Screening
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment) - ONESTOP Business Registration Portal / Companies Online.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Perform a public search of the New Zealand Register of Companies through the ONESTOP 'Name Check' facility. Verify that the proposed name complies with s 20 of the Companies Act 1993 (not undesirable, not identical, and not confusingly similar to an existing reserved or registered name) and that the legal-form suffix 'Limited' or 'Ltd' is included. Screen the proposed name against the Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand (IPONZ) trade-mark register to reduce passing-off risk. Submit the proposed name electronically through Companies Online; no filing fee applies for the availability check, though a name may be conditionally reserved in the same online session.
required_dossiers: Three proposed company names in order of preference
Identification details of each subscriber and director for the name screening
List of any corresponding overseas trade-mark registrations to assess name conflict
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a refusal under s 20 on the grounds of offensiveness or similarity, the formation agent may either file a written reconsideration request with the Companies Office or immediately elect an alternative name from the reserved list; if a third-party objection is filed, the applicant may pass a change-of-name resolution and re-submit the incorporation application within the statutory response window.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Execution of Constitutional and Governance Dossiers
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Company subscribers together with the formation agent and a New Zealand-licensed legal practitioner (no governmental filing at this stage).
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the optional constitution under s 26 of the Companies Act 1993, setting out share classes, pre-emption rights, director powers, indemnities, seat of control and dispute-resolution terms; alternatively, adopt the default statutory rules by filing no constitution. Circulate the draft constitution, the share-subscription and allotment schedule, the registered-office address consent, and the director consent forms among the subscribers. Execute all documents by wet or electronic signature permitted under the Electronic Transactions Act 2002 and retain originals in the AML/CFT customer due-diligence file maintained by the formation agent.
required_dossiers: Signed constitution (if adopted)
Share subscription and allotment schedule identifying each shareholder, number of shares and agreed consideration
Consent of the landlord or occupier to the use of the registered office address
Consent to act as director (s 151)
AML/KYC identification pack for each director and shareholder (certified passport, proof of residential address, source of funds)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: No governmental remedy applies to private drafting; if the Registrar later queries the constitution or consents, the board may adopt corrective special resolutions under s 115 and re-submit the amended documents to the Companies Office.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Statutory Filing of the Incorporation Application (Form 1)
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office - Companies Online / ONESTOP (Registrar of Companies).
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log in to Companies Online as the authorised agent; complete Form 1 (Application for Registration of a Company) by entering the company name, the limited-liability statement, the New Zealand physical registered-office address, each director's full name and residential address, the share structure and initial allotments, and by attaching the constitution and all consents. Declare that the company will maintain a share register and directors' register (ss 83 and 87). Pay the statutory fee of NZD 100.00 (approximately USD 62.00) by credit card or bank debit. Submit the application; the online system performs automated validation of the name, address and director residency requirements.
required_dossiers: Completed Form 1 (s 12, Companies Act 1993)
Certified copies of passports and proof of residential address for each director and shareholder
Evidence of the registered office address (lease, ownership deed or landlord's written consent)
Consent to act as director forms
Adopted constitution in PDF (where applicable)
AML/CFT risk assessment and client due-diligence pack prepared by the formation agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Where the Registrar rejects or queries the application under s 13 (for example, incomplete addresses, invalid consents, or non-compliant name), the agent must amend and re-submit the electronic form within 10 business days of the inquiry. Telephone and email assistance is available from the Companies Office service desk; if a material registry error persists, a formal application for correction of the Register may be lodged with the Registrar.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation and New Zealand Business Number (NZBN)
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies) and the New Zealand Business Number Registrar (MBIE).
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon successful registration, retrieve the electronic Certificate of Incorporation (s 13), the automatically generated New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) under the New Zealand Business Number Act 2016, and an extract of the public Register of Companies. Verify the spelling of the company name, the registered office and director details against the filed application. Download the certificate and registry extract and file them in the corporate minute book as conclusive evidence of incorporation.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
NZBN registration notice
Register of Companies extract
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the certificate contains a clerical error in the company name, registered office or director details, lodge a request for correction to the Register with the Companies Office online; if the NZBN is not triggered automatically within one business day, contact the MBIE business-number help desk to reactivate or manually issue the identifier.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registration with Inland Revenue (Company IRD Number, GST and Employer Obligations)
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Te Tari Taake) - myIR online portal; ONESTOP integrated business registration may be used.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File the company tax-registration application (IR 811 / entity registration) through myIR or the ONESTOP 'Business Registration' service, disclosing the intended business activity as multilingual customer helpdesk and outbound tele-sales BPO (ISIC 7820 / NAICS 561422), the proposed financial year-end, and estimated first-year turnover. Elect GST registration if annual turnover is expected to exceed NZD 60,000 (mandatory) or voluntarily for B2B input-credit recovery. If the company will hire staff in New Zealand, register as an employer for PAYE and KiwiSaver simultaneously. The IRD number is typically issued within one to three business days.
required_dossiers: Company IRD number application (IR 811 / myIR entity registration)
Certificate of Incorporation and NZBN
Forecast annual turnover and description of services
Tax residency details of each director and shareholder
Company bank account details for GST refunds and tax payments
PAYE and KiwiSaver registration data if employees will be engaged
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD application is placed 'on hold' for identity verification, respond to myIR secure-message requests with certified identity records and proof of the registered office; if the IRD number is not allocated, escalate by telephone to the IRD Business Helpline (0800 377 774). A late or incorrect registration may be cured by filing an amended IR 811 without penalty where no tax returns have yet been filed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Adoption of Registered Office and Statutory Register Bookkeeping
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Company board together with the New Zealand Companies Office for any registered-office filings.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Confirm that the registered office is an actual physical address in New Zealand at which documents may be served (s 189); postal boxes are not permitted as the sole registered office. Inaugurate the statutory registers: share register (s 83), directors' register (s 87) and directors' interests register (s 140). If the board's chosen physical address differs from the address filed in Form 1, file a notice of change of registered office with the Companies Office immediately. Keep the registers either in hard copy at the registered office or in authenticated electronic form accessible from the registered office.
required_dossiers: Registered office lease or letter of authority from the occupier
Share register (s 83)
Directors' register (s 87)
Directors' interests register (s 140)
Minute book containing the first board resolutions
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar serves a notice that the company has no effective registered office, remedy the default by filing a notice of change of registered office within 10 working days; penalties may be avoided by voluntary compliance before the Registrar takes formal enforcement action.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Compliance Calendar and Industrial/Occupational Clearance Review
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Company directors; New Zealand Companies Office; Inland Revenue; WorkSafe New Zealand; Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) and the relevant local territorial authority where physical premises are used.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Calendar the company's first annual return (due on each incorporation anniversary), GST returns (monthly or six-monthly per election), and income-tax returns (due seven months after balance date), and assess eligibility for the small-company financial-reporting exemptions under ss 200-202 of the Companies Act 1993. For the remote BPO call-centre operation (NAICS 561422 / ISIC 7820), confirm that no industrial operating permit is required. Where any physical contact-centre is established, arrange a FENZ means-of-escape and fire-system check, obtain a building warrant of fitness under the Building Act 2004, and adopt a WorkSafe workplace health-and-safety and first-aid policy under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.
required_dossiers: Annual return and tax return due-date calendar
GST registration confirmation and first filing date
FENZ fire-safety clearance or building warrant of fitness (if physical premises)
WorkSafe New Zealand workplace health-and-safety statement
Professional indemnity and cyber-insurance certificates
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a compliance filing is missed, remedy the default by filing the overdue return or document under the late-filing penalty policies of Inland Revenue or the Companies Office and request remission where reasonable cause exists. Where FENZ or WorkSafe issues a compliance notice, implement the hazard-correction or structural-rectification plan and submit evidence of abatement within the prescribed timeframe to avoid enforcement prosecution.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No industrial licensing authority is engaged for a remote BPO call-centre operation under ISIC 7820 / NAICS 561422. If a physical contact centre is later established in New Zealand, the competent authorities would be the relevant local territorial authority (building and resource consents under the Building Act 2004 and Resource Management Act 1991) together with WorkSafe New Zealand for occupational licensing and inspection.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not applicable - no statutory operating, manufacturing or call-centre licence is required in New Zealand for inbound helpdesk and outbound tele-sales BPO services. The company may elect non-statutory certifications such as ISO 27001 or a contact-centre quality standard for commercial credibility, but none is legally mandated.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand, with local territorial authorities administering land-use and discharge matters under the Resource Management Act 1991.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Category: Permitted activity - no EIA designation. A remote office-based call-centre and tele-sales operation does not trigger a full Environmental Impact Assessment, an Assessment of Environmental Effects, or a resource consent under the Resource Management Act 1991, unless premises contain generating plant, refrigerated cooling towers or other discharge-related infrastructure.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable for standard office operations - no process wastewater, volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions or hazardous waste streams are generated. General compliance thresholds include: no offensive or objectionable discharge to air, land or water (RMA 1991, s 15); proper e-waste and packaging disposal under the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and applicable product-stewardship regulations; and compliance with the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality if any emergency diesel generator or HVAC plant is installed.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: For any physical call-centre premises: Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) fire-safety clearance including means-of-escape verification under the Fire and Emergency New Zealand Act 2017; building warrant of fitness and compliance schedule under the Building Act 2004 for fire-suppression and life-safety systems; and a WorkSafe New Zealand occupational health-and-safety statement, first-aid arrangements, welfare facilities and injury-reporting protocols under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015. For the pure remote-work BPO model, a workplace health-and-safety policy, home-office work-station standard, emergency-continuity plan and IT-security framework are implemented voluntarily as good governance practice; no separate occupational licence is required.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue / IRD / Te Tari Taake), digital services portal: myIR (myir.ird.govt.nz); statutory website: www.ird.govt.nz.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate the International Company (CK_IC) with the New Zealand Companies Office, obtaining a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN); the NZBN synchronises with Inland Revenue, triggering automatic allocation of a company IRD number. Step 2: If no automatic allocation occurs, submit Form IR596 ('Registration for a company') or complete online registration through the myIR portal, supplying the certificate of incorporation, registered office address, and New Zealand-appointed agent/resident agent details. Step 3: Register for GST using Form IR356 (online via myIR or paper) once taxable supplies exceed, or forecast to exceed, NZD 60,000 in a rolling 12-month period, or elect voluntary GST registration to claim input credits. Step 4: For a non-resident head company without a fixed establishment in New Zealand, apply for a limited-purpose IRD number under sections 24F-24H of the Tax Administration Act 1994 for withholding, PAYE, or GST compliance only. Step 5: Maintain the tax registration data through myIR, appointing an IRD-accredited tax agent to manage filings, refunds, and correspondence.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a US-style check-the-box regime. Available statutory elections: (1) Look-Through Company (LTC) election under sections HA 4-HA 7 of the Income Tax Act 2007, available to close companies with five or fewer owners, allowing fiscal transparency for domestic tax purposes; (2) Active Income Exemption (AIE) election for controlled foreign company (CFC) active business income under sections DN 2 and EX 20B, exempting qualifying active income from attribution; (3) branch equivalent tax (BET) elections harmonising foreign branch tax treatment; (4) hybrid and branch mismatch elections under Part FM (inserted by the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018), permitting alignment of New Zealand treatment for hybrid financial instruments, hybrid payers, and reverse hybrids; (5) GST cash-basis election and monthly filing frequency elections for working-capital optimisation; and (6) consolidated grouping and loss offset elections (section IC 5) for wholly-owned corporate groups.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST), a destination-based consumption value added tax levied under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies (including remote services) in a rolling 12-month period, pursuant to section 51 and section 54(1A) of the GST Act 1985; voluntary registration permitted below this threshold; the NZD 60,000 threshold applies equally to non-resident suppliers of remote services to New Zealand consumers.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory real-time fiscal clearance or digital stamping exists in New Zealand. E-invoicing is voluntary, operating on the PEPPOL BIS 3.0 network through certified service providers (CSPs) and the NZBN; invoices are not pre-cleared by Inland Revenue. GST returns must be filed electronically via myIR or accredited software, and Inland Revenue operates a digital-first compliance model with payday PAYE reporting; no API clearance step is triggered at invoice issuance, but an auditable invoice trail must be preserved under section 24G of the Tax Administration Act 1994.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Section 11(1) of the GST Act 1985 zero-rates services supplied to a non-resident recipient outside New Zealand at the time of supply, unless the services are supplied in connection with land or moveable goods situated in New Zealand or are supplied to a non-resident physically present in New Zealand. Section 11A additionally zero-rates 'remote services' supplied to non-resident businesses (B2B) irrespective of place of consumption. The offshore BPO call-centre service constitutes a zero-rated supply when delivered under a cross-border contract to an offshore principal; the supplier must evidence the non-resident identity of the counterparty, the offshore place of acceptance, and the absence of New Zealand nexus of the recipient.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (via New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window; CUSDEC number)
Bill of Lading (ocean) or Air Waybill (airfreight)
Inward Remittance Certificate or SWIFT MT103/MT202 evidencing FX repatriation of the export proceeds
Executed Service Agreement / Master Services Agreement and Client Purchase Order confirming the non-resident recipient and offshore place of supply
Zero-rated GST invoice and bank/Wise B2B payment ledger confirmation
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may reassess a zero-rated supply within four years of the date of the GST assessment, extended to eight years for fraud or wilful misrepresentation (section 108, Tax Administration Act 1994). Where zero-rating is denied, the entire GST becomes payable, input credits are clawed back with use-of-money interest, and shortfall penalties apply under section 141: 20% for lack of reasonable care, 40% for an unacceptable tax position, 50% for an abusive tax position, and 100% (or 150% in deterrent cases) for evasion. Fraudulent export zero-rating claims also expose directors and the tax agent to criminal prosecution, fines up to NZD 50,000, and disqualification orders.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua), established under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 and today governed principally by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021, which regulates all registered banks in New Zealand. For AML/CFT purposes, the Reserve Bank is the supervisor for registered banks, the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) supervises non-bank financial product providers and financial advisers, and the Department of Internal Affairs supervises money remitters and other non-bank financial institutions, all under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009. The IC is also subject to the Overseas Investment Act 2015 only if it acquires sensitive land or significant business assets above the statutory threshold (NZD 100 million for most non-Government investors), which a remote BPO call-center vehicle does not trigger.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand maintains a fully liberalised, free-floating exchange-rate regime with no exchange controls. The New Zealand Dollar (NZD) is freely convertible on both current-account and capital-account transactions, and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand imposes no restrictions on the purchase, sale, or holding of foreign currency. Profit remittance and capital repatriation by a non-resident-owned international company (IC) are unrestricted, subject to three practical hurdles: (i) the standard non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) of 30% on dividends, interest and royalties, reducible under an applicable double-tax agreement (commonly 15% for portfolio dividends and 5% for substantial corporate shareholders); (ii) the bank's obligation to file International Transaction Reporting (ITR) with the Reserve Bank for reportable cross-border instructions, which is purely statistical and not a consent gate; and (iii) sufficient AML/CFT documentation of the beneficial owner and the source of funds at the receiving bank. The GST Act 1985 zero-rates exported services supplied to a non-resident recipient situated outside New Zealand, so an offshore BPO receiving fees from overseas clients will normally hold zero-rated GST status rather than being subject to domestic 15% GST output tax. There are no negative carry, exchange-holding, or approval requirements applicable to invoicing in USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, or NZD.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. New Zealand law and RBNZ prudential regulations impose no statutory export-proceeds surrender obligation, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no repatriation timeline for export receipts or service-export proceeds, including BPO call-center revenue. The IC may retain 100% of its foreign-currency earnings in any designated offshore account or in a foreign-currency account at a New Zealand registered bank without RBNZ approval. The only compliance duty is the Reporting Entity's automated International Transaction Reporting (ITR) to the Reserve Bank for individual transactions above NZD 50,000 and the IC's own income- and transfer-pricing disclosure under the Tax Administration Act 1994. A remote BPO that invoices clients abroad and pays costs, salaries, and fees from a foreign-currency operational account is outside any surrender regime.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Primary Operational Multi-Currency Account (NZD, USD, EUR, GBP, AUD) with SWIFT direct connect; optional Capital Escrow Account for share-subscription proceeds

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Bank of New Zealand (BNZ), a National Australia Bank subsidiary
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account with Corporate Treasury and FXC (FX Hedging) line; segregated USD clearing account via BMO/Correspondent

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: ASB Bank Limited, a Commonwealth Bank of Australia subsidiary
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (NZD/USD) with corporate card programme for BPO agent expense reload and payroll interface
Operational Account and International Trade Settlement Account (services/invoice settlement; standby LC issuance)
Operational Account (NZD only; retail and SME focus; strict policy on offshore-owned ICs)
Multi-Currency Global Treasury Account and Escrow/Onshore facility for integrated global cash pooling

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: HIGH for auxiliary settlement rails but MEDIUM-LOW as the sole or primary treasury account. Wise Business (Wise Payments NZ Limited, supervised by the Department of Internal Affairs as a money remitter under the AML/CFT Act 2009) and Airwallex (Airwallex (NZ) Limited, also DIA-registered; Airwallex Pty Ltd holds an Australian AFSL) can provide virtual multi-currency accounts with US ABA routing, UK sort code, EU IBAN, and local receiving numbers in 30+ corridors, enabling low-cost, interbank-rate FX and fast cross-border payments in the exact target rails (Wise_B2B and Wire_Transfer). Legal constraints: (i) an EMI is not a 'registered bank' under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 and cannot take deposits from the public; all customer funds are pooled into a segregated trust/omnibus account held at a partner Tier-1 bank, creating a credit and operational risk on the EMI itself; (ii) an EMI cannot issue an MT760 standby letter of credit, performance bond, or bank guarantee, which may be required by enterprise BPO clients; (iii) counterparties and the IC's own auditors may require a regulated-bank SWIFT MT103 trail for capital injection, invoice settlement, and profit distribution, which an EMI virtual account cannot fully replace; (iv) the EMI's own KYC and sanctions screening remains independently triggered by NZ law but the EMI will generally require a pre-funded balance from a primary regulated bank. Recommended architecture: ANZ or BNZ as the bank of record for capital, escrow, treasury, and compliance; Wise Business and/or Airwallex as the secondary high-frequency disbursement rail for agent payroll and small-vendor payments.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical presence is generally REQUIRED for at least one director (typically the executive signing director with registered authority) for the initial corporate banking onboarding interview at the chosen bank's Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch corporate banking centre, because the IC is non-resident-owned, tax-exempt, and has no established onshore trading record. ANZ, BNZ, ASB, and Westpac each apply this standard deviation for offshore international companies. Remote opening is possible but more restrictive: the bank may accept a video-based interview where all directors are located in a FATF-equivalent jurisdiction, provided each director's identity is certified by a New Zealand lawyer or notary public using apostilled or notarised passport copies, a bank reference from a top-100 global bank is supplied, and the Certificate of Incorporation, Memorandum of Association, and Resolution of Opening are legalised. Where the bank relies on a 'trusted third party' under section 30 of the AML/CFT Act 2009, that third party must be a Schedule 3 entity (e.g., a New Zealand law firm, accounting firm, or another registered bank). In practice, in-person onboarding with a named director present at the bank's Auckland CBD office shortens onboarding to 10–15 business days, while a fully remote process takes 6–8 weeks and will trigger enhanced due diligence if expected annual turnover exceeds NZD 2 million.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Tax-exempt International Company (IC) structure with no onshore substance, no local employees, no lease, and no local board activity, raising concern of round-tripping, artificial arrangement, or shell-company usage for tax evasion.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Submit (i) Certificate of Incorporation and current registry extract; (ii) the IC's tax-exempt ruling or non-resident tax status certificate issued by the Cook Islands International Company or equivalent authority; (iii) an economic-substance memorandum covering the BPO management agreement with the offshore operating centre, the 12-month payroll projection, the registered-office lease, and audited financial statements (where applicable); (iv) an executive summary of the commercial value chain from the overseas end-client to the call-centre agents; and (v) a signed declaration that the IC does not participate in any tax evasion scheme.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: UBO opacity: non-resident natural persons holding 25% or more of the IC, particularly where the ultimate owner sits in a FATF-grey-listed or non-cooperative jurisdiction or where the share register is non-public.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide (i) a fully completed UBO chart with passport copies, residential addresses, and percentage holdings; (ii) a bank reference for each UBO from a financial institution of good standing; (iii) CRS/FATCA self-certification (Form W-8BEN-E) for each non-resident owner; (iv) confirmation of no bearer shares (prohibited under the Cook Islands International Companies Act 1981-82) and no un-disclosed nominee; (v) a source-of-wealth affidavit supported by three years of bank, brokerage, or employment records; and (vi) a statement that no UBO is a sanctioned person.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Transaction-pattern mismatch: large inbound wire labelled 'capital injection' without a matching share allotment, or concentrated payroll to high volumes of low-wage agents in a high-risk remittance corridor (e.g., Philippines, India, Sri Lanka) with no underlying service contract.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Deliver (i) the share-subscription agreement and board resolution authorising each capital call; (ii) a twelve-month treasury forecast matched to the BPO service contracts; (iii) executed employment or outsourcing contracts with the agent labour provider, weekly payroll run schedules, and payroll audit logs; (iv) source-of-funds evidence for the share capital; (v) executed client service-level agreements and sample invoices proving genuine BPO delivery; and (vi) a written explanation of the commercial reason for each remittance corridor.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions and international-tax exposure: the IC, its directors, UBOs, or material clients appear on UN/EU/OFAC or UK sanctions lists, or the IC is registered in a jurisdiction under enhanced OECD/Inclusive Framework scrutiny for 'no or only nominal tax', prompting extra risk rating.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide (i) a no-match sanctions screening report generated from an independent database (World-Check, Dow Jones, or Refinitiv) covering all UBOs, directors, signatories, and principal clients; (ii) the IC's written sanctions-compliance policy accompanied by self-testing evidence; (iii) an economic-substance statement (employees, expenditure, premises, management activity) if the IC is registered in a low-tax jurisdiction; (iv) the commercial rationale for using the offshore IC; and (v) confirmation that the BPO does not serve sanctioned industries, defence, or entities on the New Zealand consolidated sanctions list under the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 or the Global Anti-Corruption sanctions framework.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Statutory verification failure: director(s) unable to attend in person, holding an expiring passport, using an unregulated intermediary, or not producing independent proof of address, causing the CDD to remain incomplete under the AML/CFT Act 2009.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Supply (i) an original or notarised passport with residual validity exceeding six months; (ii) proof of residential address dated within the last three months (utility bill, bank statement, or tax assessment); (iii) the Director's Self-Certification form countersigned by an authorised New Zealand lawyer or notary; (iv) an introduction letter from the director's existing bank, preferably within the same global banking group as the onboarding NZ bank; and (v) a completed Politically Exposed Person questionnaire where relevant.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant protocol for the IC's inbound equity: (1) Open the primary operational account and a nominee share-capital ledger at ANZ, BNZ, or ASB. (2) The UBO or foreign parent initiates a SWIFT MT103 (or ISO 20022 pacs.008 where the local corridor supports it) to the IC's account with Field 70 'Remittance Information' clearly stating 'EQUITY INJECTION / SHARE SUBSCRIPTION / [IC NAME]'. Field 50K identifies the ordering bank; Field 59 identifies the IC as final beneficiary with its NZ account number. (3) Purpose code: select the Reserve Bank's International Transaction Reporting category for balance-of-payments 'Direct Investment - Equity Capital' (commonly BOP code 518 or the bank's internal equivalent); the NZ receiving bank auto-files the ITR to the RBNZ without any consent. (4) Verification bundle filed with the bank at or before arrival of funds: board resolution authorising the share issue; share-subscription agreement; updated share register evidencing allotment; CRS/FATCA self-certifications; and the source-of-funds affidavit. (5) The bank releases funds immediately once the payment descriptor matches; no RBNZ approval is required for amounts below the significant business assets consent threshold (NZD 100 million). To avoid EDD, the remitting account should be the UBO's personal or parent-company account at a top-100 global bank, never an unregulated money remitter or an opaque third party. The IC must ensure the share capital is economically genuine and consistent with its BPO working-capital plan.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Clearing rails available: (A) SWIFT MT103 -- primary rail for BPO service settlements, overseas vendor payments, and profit repatriation; the NZ bank debits the IC's account, applies its published FX margin if converting from NZD, and routes via correspondent clearing (US Fedwire/CHIPS for USD, SEPA Instant for EUR, CHAPS for GBP, and local ACH for AUD). (B) Commercial Letters of Credit (MT700/MT707) -- not the ordinary rail for a service BPO, but a standby letter of credit (SBLC) issued by the NZ bank in favour of the IC's large enterprise clients is permissible as a performance security under ICC UCP600, supported by the IC's credit line and collateral. (C) New Zealand domestic payments -- NZD payroll and local operating expenses clear via Payments NZ's Bulk Electronic Clearing System (BECS) or the ISO 20022-based real-time rail; a zero-balancing account structure should be set up with the Tier-1 bank to sweep surplus to the primary treasury account. (D) Wise Business / Airwallex -- for high-frequency, low-value disbursements (offshore agent payroll in PHP, IDR, LKR, ZAR, or USD), the IC tops up the EMI balance via SWIFT from the primary bank, then initiates local ACH or Faster Payments; every beneficiary must be pre-screened through the EMI's sanctions engine. (E) Profit repatriation -- an MT103 referencing 'DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION / [IC NAME]' from the NZ bank to the parent/UBO account abroad, with the bank applying NRWT at the applicable DTA rate after the IC supplies Form IR67 and the foreign tax-residency certificate. Treasury discipline: transactions exceeding NZD 10,000 equivalent must carry the beneficiary's BIC and full account/IBAN; the IC's two-signatory mandate should be set at NZD 50,000, with amounts above that requiring the board's approval.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX Forwards -- NZD/USD, NZD/EUR, NZD/AUD, and NZD/GBP with tenors up to 12 months, executed with ANZ, BNZ, ASB, or Westpac under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement or a bank FX facilities line; the IC must satisfy the eligible/wholesale investor test under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) -- permitted only for soft or non-deliverable currencies where no active NZD offshore deliverable market exists, e.g., PHP/NZD, IDR/NZD, VND/NZD, used to hedge the BPO's offshore wage cost; structured through the NZ bank's regional desk; not used for NZD itself because NZD is freely deliverable.

Cross-Currency Swaps and FX Swaps -- available for converting USD-denominated BPO receivables into NZD or for hedging the principal of the equity injection; requires ISDA plus Credit Support Annex and a board-approved hedge policy.

Vanilla FX Options -- call and put options on NZD/USD and NZD/EUR with limited premium risk, suitable for protecting contingent multi-currency tender flows and invoice pipeline volatility; permitted only where the IC is classified as an 'eligible investor' or the hedging is incidental to its genuine trading business.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return under Companies Act 1993, Section 209 (confirmation of registered office, directors, members and shareholding)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies), Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Each year, within 20 working days after the anniversary of the date of incorporation; the Companies Office issues a reminder before the anniversary date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Default triggers a reminder and formal notice; continued non-filing permits the Registrar to initiate removal under Section 213 of the Companies Act 1993, leading to administrative strike-off after statutory notice periods. Non-compliance is an offence under Section 363 with fines up to NZD 10,000; property of a struck-off company vests in the Crown.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Audited Financial Statements and Regulatory Filing for FMC Reporting or 'Large' Entities under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 (conditional; not triggered for the current small remote BPO entity)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (for public filing when mandatory); otherwise audited financial statements are provided to shareholders and retained for seven years.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: When triggered, audited financial statements must be filed within five months of the balance date (for a 31 March balance date, by 31 August); while the entity is exempt, no annual filing deadline applies.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Not currently applicable. If the entity later qualifies as large or as an FMC reporting entity, failure to audit or file is an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, with fines up to NZD 10,000 per director and continuing monthly penalties.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit applies to FMC reporting entities under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and to 'large' companies under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 (approximately total assets exceeding NZD 60 million, total annual revenue exceeding NZD 30 million, or more than 50 full-time equivalent employees; exact classification per Section 45). The subject remote BPO entity operates below these thresholds and is exempt from compulsory audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Financial statements are prepared under New Zealand Generally Accepted Accounting Practice as set by the External Reporting Board: NZ IFRS for Tier 1; NZ IFRS with Reduced Disclosure Regime (Tier 2) for private companies; simplified accrual standards for small non-FMC entities.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand operates a single annual confirmation regime: the annual return must verify the register of members, share transfers during the year, and current directors and registered office details. Director changes must be lodged with the Companies Office within 10 working days; shareholding changes are recorded in the statutory register of members and confirmed at the next annual return. No separate public UBO filing exists for non-FSP companies, but internal beneficial-ownership records must be maintained and retained for seven years for AML/KYC integrity.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Members, Register of Directors, Minute Book

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 500 - 1,500 per annum (NZD 800 - 2,500) for a local registered office address and corporate service provider / registered agent.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 8,000 - 16,000 per engagement (NZD 12,000 - 25,000); estimated only, as the entity is below the compulsory audit thresholds and no audit is currently required.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: New Zealand does not generally grant statutory tax holidays or preferential corporate income tax rates to non-resident International Companies engaged in offshore BPO/call-centre services. Income derived by a non-resident from offshore services is generally not subject to New Zealand corporate income tax unless derived through a New Zealand fixed establishment or the non-resident is otherwise carrying on business in New Zealand through a dependent agent constituting a permanent establishment. No specific call-centre or BPO tax incentive exists under the Income Tax Act 2007. However, a 20% research and development tax credit may be available for eligible R&D activity, which is not applicable to standard call-centre services. The effective tax rate for an IC deriving only foreign-sourced income with no New Zealand fixed establishment is effectively 0% for non-resident income not sourced in New Zealand.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Non-resident companies without a New Zealand fixed establishment are generally not required to file a New Zealand income tax return (IR4) unless New Zealand-sourced income is derived. If a New Zealand fixed establishment exists, the IR4 Company Income Tax Return must be filed through myIR, the Inland Revenue online portal.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard balance date of 31 March, the IR4 return is due by 7 July following the end of the income year (automated extension to 31 March of the following year if the return is filed by a tax agent with an extension of time arrangement). For a non-standard balance date, the deadline is generally the 7th day of the fourth month after the balance date, subject to tax agent extensions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income derived during the income year from all sources, including New Zealand-sourced income attributable to a fixed establishment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident ICs with no fixed establishment enter nil for New Zealand-sourced income; foreign-sourced income derived wholly offshore is not taxable in New Zealand and may be omitted.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total expenses incurred in deriving the income, including operating costs of the New Zealand fixed establishment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter only deductible expenses attributable to the New Zealand permanent establishment; offshore BPO labour and technology costs not attributable to the fixed establishment are excluded.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income or loss before tax credits and imputation credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident IC with no New Zealand fixed establishment, enter zero taxable income. Where a fixed establishment exists, net income attributable to that New Zealand operation is calculated under ordinary New Zealand tax rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax payable calculated at the company tax rate of 28% on net taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the 28% rate only to New Zealand-sourced taxable income attributable to a fixed establishment. If no fixed establishment exists, tax payable is nil.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credit account (ICA) credit balance attached to dividends paid to shareholders.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident shareholders cannot generally receive imputation credits; the IC should enter only credits attaching to dividends paid to New Zealand-resident shareholders, and must maintain ICA records if dividends are paid.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loss offsets brought forward from prior income years.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident ICs may only offset losses that arose from New Zealand-sourced activity and that satisfy continuity of ownership rules. Offshore losses are unavailable.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Resident withholding tax (RWT) and other tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident ICs should enter New Zealand RWT withheld from interest or other investment income; no RWT applies to pure offshore BPO service revenue.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax payable after credits, being the final net tax position.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Where no New Zealand income is returned, the final tax payable is zero, and no payment is required.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalties apply under the Tax Administration Act 1994. The initial failure-to-file penalty is NZ$250 for small businesses or NZ$500 for non-small businesses, increasing by NZ$250/NZ$500 for each further month of non-compliance, capped at NZ$1,000/NZ$2,000 per return period. In addition, late payment of tax attracts an initial late payment penalty of 1% of unpaid tax, followed by an additional 4% after 7 days and a further 1% per month for up to three months, plus interest on unpaid tax (currently 10.94% per annum for underpaid tax, as at the applicable quarterly rate). Knowingly filing a false or misleading return can trigger criminal penalties and shortfall penalties of up to 150% of the tax shortfall.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The statutory non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) rate on dividends paid by a New Zealand company to a non-resident shareholder is 30% subject to reduction under an applicable double tax agreement (DTA).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke treaty relief and reduce NRWT on dividends paid to non-resident shareholders, the non-resident recipient must complete and provide a New Zealand IR871 (Certificate of Non-Resident Tax Rate Entitlement) to the New Zealand company before the dividend is paid. The IR871 requires disclosure of the shareholder's country of residence, entitlement to DTA benefits, and confirmation that the shareholder is not simply a conduit for a person not entitled to treaty benefits. The New Zealand payer must retain the IR871 as evidence for the reduced rate. No advance ruling from Inland Revenue is generally required where the treaty claim is standard. A Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by the shareholder's residence country must be available upon request to satisfy Inland Revenue that the recipient is fiscally resident in the treaty jurisdiction. The IC must also ensure the payee has 'economic substance' in the residence jurisdiction or otherwise satisfies any limitation-on-benefits or principal-purpose test under the relevant DTA to prevent treaty shopping denial. Where the DTA does not apply, the full 30% NRWT rate must be withheld and paid to Inland Revenue by the 20th day of the month following the payment.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: The statutory NRWT rate for interest is 15% (or 2% for interest paid to certain non-resident financial institutions under approved arrangements) and the statutory rate for royalties is 15%. Under New Zealand's DTA with the United Kingdom (applicable to Cook Islands International Companies where tax residency is structured through the UK or other treaty jurisdictions), the treaty rate for interest is generally 10% (and in many cases 0% for interest paid to a government or financial institution), while the royalty rate is generally 10%, provided the recipient is the beneficial owner. Australia and other DTA partners may impose similar or different rates; the specific DTA rate depends on the shareholder/lender's residence jurisdiction. Approvals for reduced rates are obtained via the IR871 process as above; for royalties, New Zealand also requires approved issuer levy (AIL) considerations, though AIL is not generally applicable to dividend, interest, or royalty NRWT and is instead a levy on certain interest payments made to non-residents by approved issuers.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand's transfer pricing rules under Subpart GC and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines apply to cross-border related-party transactions. The master file (MTF) and local file (LTF) documentation thresholds are NZ$10 million for the aggregate value of cross-border related-party transactions for the income year, excluding dividend payments. Where the threshold is exceeded, the company must prepare and maintain a master file and a local file in accordance with Inland Revenue's Transfer Pricing Guidelines, and submit a TP disclosure statement (IR1061) with the income tax return. Documentation must be contemporaneous and demonstrate arm's length pricing. For BPO/call-centre services, the analysis must benchmark the service fee against comparable uncontrolled service providers, considering functions, assets, and risks of the New Zealand entity versus the related offshore service provider.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand has not enacted standalone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) equivalent to the UAE or Bermuda models. However, the economic substance doctrine is applied through several statutory channels: (1) the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) in section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, which voids tax avoidance arrangements lacking commercial substance; (2) New Zealand's controlled foreign company (CFC) rules and foreign investment fund (FIF) rules, which may attribute income from low-tax offshore entities; (3) the requirement under many DTAs that treaty benefits require the recipient to be the beneficial owner, subject to the Principle Purpose Test (PPT) under the OECD Multilateral Instrument (MLI); and (4) Inland Revenue's ability to treat an entity as having a permanent establishment in New Zealand if it has substantive New Zealand-based activities. A Cook Islands International Company or other offshore IC must therefore demonstrate genuine non-resident substance, including substantive decision-making outside New Zealand, non-resident directors, physical office presence outside New Zealand, and arm's-length payments, to avoid re-characterisation of its income as New Zealand-sourced or as a sham.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and Fraudulent Tax Returns
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly failing to file a required IR4 return, omitting New Zealand-sourced income attributable to a New Zealand fixed establishment, fabricating expenses, or providing false IR871 certificates to Inland Revenue to obtain treaty benefits to which the entity is not entitled.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: A tax evasion conviction under the Tax Administration Act 1994 section 143B carries a maximum fine of NZ$50,000 for an individual, or NZ$250,000 for a company, for each offence. The court may also order payment of the tax shortfall plus penalties and interest. Shortfall penalties for gross carelessness or intentional disregard can range from 20% to 150% of the tax shortfall. For 2024-2025, the use-of-money interest rate on underpayments is 10.94% per annum.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for the company's tax liabilities via the director tax liability provisions in the Tax Administration Act 1994 if tax is not paid within 10 working days of a demand and the company has no reasonable prospect of paying. The Commissioner may seek a court order for recovery against directors personally. Criminal liability may extend to directors and officers who aided, abetted, or were knowingly concerned in the evasion, exposing them to fines of up to NZ$50,000 and potential imprisonment for evasion offences. Under s 143B, a person who knowingly assists in evading tax is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years for tax evasion (punishable on conviction on indictment), along with fines. Additionally, a director may be personally liable for civil penalties under the Companies Act 1993 and be prohibited from managing companies if found to have acted fraudulently or recklessly.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Artificial Arrangement Lacking Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a Cook Islands International Company or similar New Zealand-linked offshore vehicle as a bare legal titleholder with no real commercial activity, no physical presence outside New Zealand, no substantive decision-making, and services performed entirely in New Zealand for the economic benefit of New Zealand residents, resulting in tax avoidance or a sham.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The arrangement may be voided under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (s BG 1 and s GA 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007). Inland Revenue may reconstruct the arrangement, assess tax as if the arrangement had not been entered into, impose a shortfall penalty of up to 100% of the resulting tax shortfall for dominant purpose of tax avoidance, and charge interest from the date the original tax liability arose. The company may also be liable for a late payment penalty and receive a court order requiring dissolution or deregistration. If the shell is used to evade tax, criminal fines up to NZ$250,000 apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of a shell company who caused the company to enter into an arrangement for a dominant tax avoidance purpose may be personally liable for the company's tax shortfall under the director penalty notice regime. Where the arrangement is a sham at common law, the corporate veil will be pierced and directors and controlling shareholders will be personally liable for the tax owed plus penalties. Under the Companies Act 1993, directors who act dishonestly in relation to the company may be ordered to pay compensation, and a court may disqualify them from being a director for up to 5 years or more for persistent contraventions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Anti-Terrorism Financing (CTF) Compliance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the BPO/call-centre company's banking or payment rails (Wise B2B and wire transfers) to process client funds or personal remuneration in a manner that obscures the beneficial owner, facilitates undisclosed third-party payments, or accepts proceeds derived from foreign predicate offences; or failing to maintain a compliant AML/CTF programme under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 if the business activity falls within the definition of a 'financial service' (e.g., providing money or value transmission services, foreign exchange, or acting as a payment gateway).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the AML/CTF Act 2009, an offence committed by a body corporate for most strict liability offences carries a maximum fine of NZ$2 million per offence, and calculation errors of suspicious transaction reports can trigger separate penalties. For serious and knowing money laundering offences under the Crimes Act 1961 section 243, an individual is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 7 years, and a body corporate is liable to a fine not exceeding NZ$1 million. Failure to report suspicious transactions can also attract civil liability and compliance costs plus penalties under the Financial Markets Authority or Department of Internal Revenue enforcement actions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior managers who knowingly authorised, permitted, or failed to take reasonable steps to prevent the company's AML/CTF breaches can be prosecuted individually. Under the AML/CTF Act, a director may be fined up to NZ$2 million for a body corporate offence if the offence is attributable to the director's wilful neglect. Money laundering convictions can result in imprisonment of the individual director for up to 7 years. A travel ban may be imposed by court order when a custodial sentence is anticipated for non-resident directors. Directors may also be subject to civil asset forfeiture under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Non-Compliance and Documentation Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to maintain a transfer pricing master file/local file when the NZ$10 million cross-border related-party transaction threshold is exceeded; pricing intercompany service fees or management charges for the BPO/call-centre without an arm's length benchmark; using a cost-plus margin below the lower quartile of comparables without justification; or failing to include a contemporaneous economic analysis at a date later than the income tax return filing deadline.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue may adjust the taxable income under the arm's length principle, applying the transfer pricing rules in Subpart GC and section GD 13. Transfer pricing shortfall penalties apply under section 141FB of the Tax Administration Act 1994. A 100% shortfall penalty applies where the taxpayer's gross transfer pricing adjustment exceeds NZ$2.5 million and the taxpayer had both a 'dominant purpose' of avoiding tax and failed to retain adequate documentation. Lower penalties of 20% or 40% may apply for not meeting the 'acceptable level of care' or 'unacceptable tax position' thresholds. Interest applies to the resulting tax shortfall from the original due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Where the transfer pricing adjustment causes tax shortfall that remains unpaid, the director penalty notice provisions in Part 11 of the Tax Administration Act 1994 allow the Commissioner to hold directors personally liable for the unpaid tax. Directors who knowingly signed a false or misleading income tax return containing TP adjustments may face evasion penalties and personal fines up to NZ$50,000, and imprisonment up to 5 years for evasion. Directors cannot rely on the in-house CFO's or external accountant's negligence where they failed to exercise reasonable diligence in overseeing the tax compliance function.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Misclassification of New Zealand Permanent Establishment
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A non-resident BPO company claiming that no New Zealand corporate income tax return is due while its remote call-centre employees, servers, or a dependent agent in New Zealand carry on core revenue-generating activities, concluding contracts of inbound/outbound call services with New Zealand clients, or maintaining a fixed place of business in New Zealand. Also, prematurely relying on a zero-effective rate without a factual PE analysis.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue will assess the company as having a New Zealand permanent establishment, attributing profits based on the OECD authorised OECD approach. The company is liable to pay income tax at 28% on the attributable New Zealand-source profits, plus use-of-money interest from the original due date and shortfall penalties for an unacceptable tax position (20%) or gross carelessness (40%) if the PE was knowingly concealed. Late filing penalties also apply for the unfiled IR4.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who make or assist in making a false declaration that no PE exists when they know or ought to know of the New Zealand substantive activity can be personally fined under tax evasion provisions and be liable for the company's unpaid tax through director penalty notices. Overseas directors may receive travel bans preventing them from leaving New Zealand if criminal proceedings are commenced, and may be subject to surrender of passports under the Bail Act 2000 in cases involving tax evasion charges.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Collect and Remit Non-Resident Withholding Tax on Repatriation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, interest, or royalties to a non-resident parent or beneficiary without deducting the proper NRWT rate (30% for dividends, 15% for interest/royalties in the absence of a reduced treaty rate); making a treaty-reduced payment without obtaining the IR871 certificate; or classifying a dividend as a management fee or loan repayment to avoid NRWT.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The company is liable as the agent of the non-resident for the withholding tax and must pay the unpaid NRWT plus penalties. The late payment penalty applies immediately to the unpaid NRWT amount, plus use-of-money interest. Shortfall penalties for failing to withhold where required are 20% of the tax shortfall if the position was not 'acceptable', and up to 150% for evasion. If the company fails to remit the withheld tax, the Commissioner may recover the amount as a debt due from the company; directors can be made personally liable.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who fail to ensure NRWT is withheld and remitted within the statutory time frames are exposed to the director penalty regime in section 56 and Part 11 of the Tax Administration Act 1994, under which personal liability is triggered if the NRWT is unpaid for more than 10 working days after the Commissioner's demand. Directors who knowingly enter into a dividend-stripping arrangement to avoid NRWT may be charged with tax evasion, leading to fines and imprisonment of up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Reportable Tax Arrangement and Disclosure Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Entering into a tax avoidance arrangement that Inland Revenue has declared a 'tax avoidance scheme' under sections 20B-20E, or participating in a 'reportable tax arrangement' (including certain loss-buying, dividend-stripping, or cross-border financing schemes) without disclosing the arrangement to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue on form IR304.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The promoter and participants of a reportable tax arrangement that is later voided by the Commissioner face shortfall penalties of up to 100% of the tax shortfall, plus possible civil penalties of up to NZ$200,000 for promoters under section 141ED. The arrangement may be cancelled and reconstructed. Inland Revenue may also apply the specific penalties regime under s 141EA for failure to disclose, with fines of up to NZ$2,000 plus 100% of any tax shortfall.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the IC who promoted, designed, or implemented the arrangement may be treated as 'promoters' and personally liable for civil penalties of up to NZ$200,000. Where the arrangement is an artificial loss scheme, the promoter may also be barred from managing a company and personal criminal liability may arise under the Crimes Act 1961 for false accounting or fraud, carrying up to 7 years imprisonment.
